Read About Arusha

A Maasai trading post that became a German fort, then a diplomatic capital, then the one town on Earth sitting on top of a gemstone found nowhere else — before most visitors ever notice, they are already on their way to the parks.

A trading town before it was a town

Arusha existed for a century before anyone built anything permanent here. In the 1830s, agro-pastoral Maasai from the Arusha Chini community south of Kilimanjaro settled the site, trading grain, honey, beer and tobacco with the pastoral Kisongo Maasai for livestock, milk, meat and hides. It was a regional exchange point, not a city, and it stayed that way for decades — a place where the highland farmers and the plains herders met in the middle. When the Pangani Valley trade route was extended through the area in the 1860s, connecting the coast to western Kenya, demand for Arusha's produce grew, and the settlement grew with it.

Nothing about that slow accumulation of trade prepared the town for what came next. In 1896, German colonial forces conquered Arusha in retaliation for the killing of two missionaries who had tried to settle on the slopes of Mount Meru. Four years later, in 1900, the Germans built a fort — a boma — on a rise overlooking the plains, garrisoned with soldiers and, by one contemporary account, a machine gun. It was, as the historical record puts it, "a solid statement, meant to impress German moral and political order on the surrounding countryside." Africans were forcibly displaced from the land and put to work digging lime and hauling stone for its walls. That building is still standing. It is the first stop most visitors make.

The fort that keeps changing hands

The Germans held Arusha for twenty years. The British took it in 1916, mid–World War I, deporting the German missionaries and settlers and leaving only a skeleton administration behind. Civilian government returned in the 1920s, American missionaries arrived, British and Greek settlers reoccupied the old German farms, and in 1928 a railway line reached Arusha from Moshi — a spur that briefly made this a connected town in a way it has not been since. The line is long gone; Arusha today has no working passenger rail at all, a fact that surprises visitors who assume a city this size must have one.

By the early 1950s Arusha was, in one visiting journalist's description, "a polyglot, westernized little town" with a Greek community, German families who had stayed on since before the first war, and German-Jewish refugees who arrived after the second. The old fort had by then become a museum — natural history, colonial history, a botanical garden grown up around the parade ground where German soldiers once drilled. Its exhibits still cover this whole arc: pre-colonial trade, conquest, and the slow accretion of a genuinely mixed town.

The fort was built to impose German order on the surrounding country. It now houses a 160-year-old tortoise and a room of stuffed wildlife.

The declaration that renamed a country's direction

Arusha's single largest claim on world history was signed here on 5 February 1967. Julius Nyerere, Tanzania's first president, used the town to announce the Arusha Declaration — a manifesto committing the newly independent country to ujamaa, African socialism built on self-reliance and collective agriculture rather than a Western development model or a Soviet one. It nationalized banks and major industries, redirected the country toward rural cooperative villages, and set Tanzania's economic and political course for the next two decades. Historians still argue about whether ujamaa succeeded, but nobody disputes that it was one of the defining experiments in post-colonial African governance, and it happened in a building a fifteen-minute walk from the old German fort.

That the declaration happened in Arusha at all was not an accident of geography. By the mid-1960s the town had already become the place where the region settled its disagreements — a role that would only deepen in the decades that followed.

The city of agreements

Arusha's official motto translates as "City of Agreements," and the nickname is earned rather than aspirational. The documents ceding Tanganyika's independence from Britain were signed here in 1961. The Arusha Accords, meant to end Rwanda's civil war, were signed here in August 1993 — an agreement that collapsed within months when the Rwandan genocide began, but whose failure led directly to the United Nations placing the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in this same town from 1994 to 2015, prosecuting the genocide's organizers in a building that still stands near the city center. A peace agreement for Burundi was signed here in 2000. A framework for reunifying South Sudan's ruling party was signed here in January 2015. Arusha today hosts the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights and serves as the administrative capital of the East African Community — a five-country bloc whose flags fly outside buildings most visitors walk past without a second look.

None of this diplomatic weight is visible from the street. Arusha does not look like a seat of continental justice. It looks like a safari town with a busy roundabout at its center, which is also true, and which is the town's actual daily business.

A stone with one address on the planet

In January 1967 — the same year as the Declaration — a man named Jumanne Mhero Ngoma found sparkling blue stones scattered across the Mererani Hills, a patch of ground about seven kilometers long and two wide at the foot of Kilimanjaro. What he had found was a previously unknown variety of the mineral zoisite, colored blue-violet by trace vanadium. Tiffany & Co., which brought the stone to market in 1968, decided "blue-violet zoisite" would never sell and renamed it tanzanite instead. It remains, to this day, found in no other economically viable deposit anywhere on Earth — one gemstone, one narrow strip of hillside, one country. Every tanzanite in every ring and pendant in the world traces back to that same stretch of ground outside Arusha.

The mining district is fenced and restricted, but the trade runs straight through town: cutting houses, certification offices and showrooms cluster around a single plaza downtown, where the stone moves from rough crystal to polished gem within a few city blocks of where Nyerere once announced a very different kind of national wealth.

Base camp, and proud of it

Arusha's other identity — the one that actually fills its hotels — is entirely geographic. The town sits below Mount Meru, Tanzania's second-highest peak, on the eastern edge of the Great Rift Valley, within a few hours' drive of Arusha National Park, Lake Manyara, the Ngorongoro Crater, Tarangire and, further on, the Serengeti. This proximity is not a recent tourism discovery. Parts of the 1962 Hollywood film Hatari!, starring John Wayne as a professional animal trapper, were shot at the Momella Lakes and on Mount Meru's slopes, inside what is now Arusha National Park — the same lakes and forest a modern visitor drives past on the way to a single day's game drive.

Arusha does not pretend to be a wildlife destination in its own right. It has simply always been the door the wildlife destinations open through.

That arrangement suits the town. Arusha has never needed to compete with the parks for a visitor's attention, and it does not try to. Its hotels assume an early alarm clock. Its restaurants keep breakfast service running before dawn. Its guides know the Ngorongoro crater rim's temperature swing better than the town's own downtown blocks, because that is the piece of local knowledge that actually gets used. A city with a two-hundred-year trading history, a fort, a declaration, a war-crimes tribunal and a gemstone found nowhere else has, in the end, settled comfortably into being the place you spend one night on your way to somewhere wilder — and it does that job better than almost anywhere else in Africa.
